RULES AND REGULATIONS
TITLE 14— CIVIL AVIATION
Chapter II—-Civil Aeronautics Admin­
istration, Department of Commerce
Part 575—F ederal Civil Airports on 
Canton and W ake I slands
Under section 10 (a) of the Interna­
tional Aviation Facilities Act, the Ad­
ministrator of Civil ‘ Aeronautics is 
empowered and directed to do and per­
form all acts and things necessary or 
incident to the operation, protection, 
maintenance, improvement, and admin­
istration of airport property in territory 
outside the continental limits of the 
United States which he has acquired pur­
suant to the act or any other provision of 
law. This includes the power to make 
and amend such reasonable rules and 
regulations as he may deem necessary 
to the proper exercise of the powers 
granted by the section, and to make just 
and reasonable charges for aeronautical 
services, including but not limited to 
landing f66S.
Acting pursuant to the foregoing au­
thority, and in accordance with section 
3 (a) (3) of the Administrative Pro­
cedure Act, Part 575 is hereby adopted. 
The charges contained in this Part have 
been established at a level which is con­
sidered to be Within the ability of civil 
aviation to pay, and will be only partially 
compensatory at this time for the costs 
to the United States Government of 
maintaining and operating the landing 
areas involved. As ability of civil avia­
tion to pay changes, the level of charges 
will be revised with a view to recovering, 
as soon as practicable, the total costs of 
maintaining and operating the- landing 
areas.
SUBPABT A— INTRODUCTION
Sec. >
575.1 Explanation of terms.
SUBPART B— LANDING AND PARKING FEES
575.11 Landing fees.
575.12 Parking fees.
675.13 Alteration of fees.
575.14 Payment of fees.
SUBPART C— LOADING AND UNLOADING AREAS
575.21 Control of areas.
A u t h o r i t y: §§ 575.1 through 575.21 Issued  
under sec. 10, 62 Stat. 453; 49 U. S. C. Sup.,  
4159.
SUBPART A — INTRODUCTION
§  575.1 Explanation of terms —(a) 
Aircraft weight.  “Aircraft weight” shall 
mean the maximum take-off weight per­
mitted by the appropriate aeronautical 
authority of the State of manufacture
13 CFR, 1945 Supp.; i0 F. R. 12419.  
* •3  CFR, 1947 Supp.; 12 F. R. 7613.
of the aircraft. It shall be calculated to 
the nearest 1,000 pounds.
(b) Airport. “Airport” shall mean 
the Canton Island airport and the Wake 
Island airport operated by the Civil Aero­
nautics "  Administration.
(c) CAA. “CAA” shall mean the Civil 
Aeronautics Administration.
SUBPART B — LANDING AND PARKING FEES
§  575.11 Landing fees— t a) Rate of  
charge. A charge of 16 cents per 1,000 
pounds shall be made for each landing 
of an aircraft at the airport. (No addi­
tional charge .for each take-off shall be 
made.)(b) Exceptions to charge.  The follow­
ing aircraft shall not be subject to land­
ing fees:(1) Civil aircraft not engaged in com­
mercial operations;
(2) Aircraft engaged in test flights. 
(This shall not include survey and 
proving runs);
(3) Aircraft compelled to return after 
take-off;-
(4) Public aircraft not engaged in 
commercial operations.
§  575.12 Parking fees— (a) Hangar 
parking fee.  A charge of 5 cents per 
1,000 pounds of aircraft weight shall be 
made for each 6-hour period or fraction 
thereof during which an aircraft is 
parked in a hangar at the airport.
(b) Outside parking fee.  A charge of 
2.5 cents per 1,000 pounds of aircraft 
weight shall be made for each 6-hour 
period or fraction thereof during which 
an aircraft is parked outside at the air­
port. The charge shall start six hours 
after the plane lands.
§  575.13 Alteration of fees.  Charges 
for-aircraft based at the airport may be 
fixed by the CAA Regional Administrator 
having jurisdiction over the airport, 
without regard to the landing and park­
ing fees provided in §§ 575.11 and 575.12.
§  575.14 Payment of fees —(a) Time 
and means of payment.  Fees shall be 
paid in United States dollars at the time 
use is made of the airport.
(b) Exceptions to time of payment.  
Scheduled air carriers and other aircraft 
operators may make prior financial ar­
rangements with the CAA official in 
charge of the airport. These arrange­
ments may include provision for pay­
ment on a monthly or other suitable 
basis.
SUBPART C — LOADING AND UNLOADING A REAS
§  575.21 Control of areas.  The CAA 
official in charge of the airport shall have 
full control of the loading and unloading 
areas to insure efficient and noh-discrim-
inatory utilization. Such authority shall 
inplude, but shall not necessarily be lim­
ited to, the right to:
(a) Assign space and sequence of use 
when lie-concludes that it is necessary 
or advisable;
(b) Order the movement of a stand­
ing aircraft to conform with assign­
ments under paragraph (a) of this 
sêction ;
(c) Assess an excess parking fee of 
$5 per hour for non-conformity with 
paragraph (b) of this section.
This part shall become effective May 1, 
1950.

Acting Administrator of  
Civil Aeronautics.

Executive Order 10123 (15 FR 2265 (Federal Register of April 22, 1950)) was signed April 20, 1950. The filing stamp printed after the order reads April 20, 1950; the held OCR prints the signing line as April 2d, 1950, which is the register's signing date of April 20, 1950 read through an OCR error. Its held Federal Register text, registered as the original representation for this order, prints the order number, its title and the signing date, and its operative command is the sentence providing that Executive Order No. 9635 and Executive Order No. 9904, which amended it, “are hereby revoked”, followed by a sentence limiting the effect of the revocation. On 2026-10-14 the command is terminated: a revoking command is complete when it takes effect, and this order states no separate effective date, so it took effect when signed on April 20, 1950. The order contains no condition, postponement, report, transfer or continuing duty. No other held text cites this order's number by an order citation. The Federal Register disposition-note search, the U.S. Code citation search and the eCFR citation search each report no hit naming this order; the last two test only for current citations and are cited as bounded searches. The surviving consequence is that Executive Order No. 9635 of September 29, 1945 (organization of the Navy Department and the Naval Establishment) and Executive Order No. 9904 of November 13, 1947, which amended it remains revoked; that consequence follows from the performed command and is not a command that still has to end.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10129 (15 FR 3499 (Federal Register of June 6, 1950)) was signed June 3, 1950. Its held Federal Register text prints the order number, the title and the signing date; the text breaks across a page after paragraph 7 and resumes on a later page of the same issue, so paragraph 7 appears in two pieces. It creates the President's Commission on Migratory Labor (paragraph 1), directs it to inquire into five subjects (paragraph 2), requires a written report by December 15, 1950 (paragraph 3), authorizes hearings (paragraph 4), directs consultation with the Department of State (paragraph 5), directs agency cooperation (paragraph 6), provides funding for the fiscal years 1950 and 1951 from the Emergency Fund for the President (paragraph 7) and provides in paragraph 8 that the Commission ceases to exist thirty days after its report unless otherwise determined by further Executive Order. On 2026-10-14 every clause is terminated on May 31, 1951, the day the Commission ceased to exist. Executive Order 10192 (15 FR 9029 (Federal Register of December 19, 1950)), signed December 15, 1950, amended paragraph 3 (the report date becomes March 1, 1951) and paragraph 8 (“Thirty days” becomes “Sixty days”). Executive Order 10236 (16 FR 3607 (Federal Register of April 27, 1951)), signed April 26, 1951, amended paragraph 8 as amended to read “The Commission shall cease to exist at the end of May 31,1951.”, which fixes the end. The report date of paragraph 3 and the report-relative cessation of paragraph 8 are not ends: the held corpus does not give the date the report was rendered, and Executive Order 10236 replaced the report-relative rule with a fixed date while the Commission still existed. Executive Order 10193's Federal Register page contains the text of Executive Order 10192 and cites Executive Order 10129 only for that reason; it is not a separate amendment. The held-text search for citations of the order found only Executive Orders 10192, 10236 and their page copies. The Federal Register disposition-note search lists two hits (the 10192 and 10236 amendments); the U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit.
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"No earlier end is shown. The only rule that could have ended the Commission earlier is paragraph 8's original report-relative cessation (thirty days, then sixty days, after the report was rendered). The held corpus does not state when the report was rendered, but Executive Order 10236 of April 26, 1951 amended paragraph 8 to a fixed date and treats the Commission as continuing to May 31, 1951; had the report-relative period already run, there would have been nothing left to amend. The date recorded is May 31, 1951; Executive Order 10236 says the Commission ceases “at the end of” that day, so the inclusive and exclusive readings coincide with the close of May 31, 1951. A report deadline is not an end, and the amendments are later events.","independent_command_check":"All pieces serve the single Commission and fall with its existence. Paragraph 7's text names fiscal years 1950 and 1951; the fiscal year 1951 outlasted the Commission's last day, but the paragraph funds the Commission's compensation and expenditures and has no operation once the Commission has ceased to exist, so it is recorded as ending with the Commission. The outer fiscal-year bound is disclosed and not used as the end.","savings_check":"The order's text has no saving clause. The Commission's report and recommendations were produced during its life and are not commands of the order; the bounded searches found no later order that continues or revives the Commission.","scope_check":"Nine operative pieces replace the dossier's thirteen fragments: paragraph 1 (with the authority recital), paragraph 2 with subparagraphs (a) to (e), paragraphs 3, 4, 5 and 6, paragraph 7 in two pieces because a page break splits it (the dossier span for it ran through a page of unrelated contents lists), and paragraph 8."}

By virtue of the authority vested in 
me as President of the United States, it 
is hereby ordered as follows:
1 . There is hereby created a Commis­
sion to be known as the President’s Com­
mission on Migratory Labor, which shall 
consist of a Chairman and four other 
members to be designated by the Presi­
dent.
2. The Commission is authorized and 
directed to inquire into
(a) social, economic, health, and edu­
cational conditions among migratory 
workers, both alien and domestic, in the 
United States;
(b) problems created by the migration 
of workers, for temporary employment, 
into the United States, pursuant to the 
immigration laws or otherwise;
(c) responsibilities now being assumed 
by Federal, State, county and municipal 
authorities with respect to alleviating 
the conditions among migratory workers, 
both alien and domestic;
(d) whether sufficient numbers of 
local and migratory workers can be ob­
tained from domestic sources to meet 
agricultural labor needs and, if not, the 
extent to which the temporary employ­
ment of foreign workers may be required 
to supplement the domestic labor supply; 
and
(e) the extent of illegal migration of 
foreign workers into the United States 
and the problems (Sreated thereby, and 
whether, and in what respect, current 
law enforcement measures and the au­
thority and means possessed by Federal, 
State, and local governments may be 
strengthened and improved to eliminate 
such illegal migration.
3. The Commission shall make a re­
port of its studies to the President in 
writing not later than December 15,1950, 
including its recommendations for Gov­
ernmental action, either legislative or 
administrative
4. In connection with its studies and 
inquiries, the Commission is authorized 
to hold such public hearings and to hear 
such witnesses as it deems appropriate.

quiries, and recommendations of the 
Commission involve considerations of 
international arrangements and policies 
the Commission shall consult with the 
Department of State.

agencies of the Federal Government are 
authorized and directed to cooperate 
with the Commission in its work and to 
furnish the Commission such informa­
tion and assistance, not inconsistent 
with law, as it may require in the per­
formance of its duties.

P art 507—Airworthiness  D irectives
M ISCELLANEO US A M END M ENTS
This amendment to Part 507 contains  
the Airworthiness Directives amended or  
issued during January 1958. Individual  
notice of the Airworthiness Directives  
contained herein has been given to 4  op­
erators and other interested persons who  
are subscribers to a Civil Aeronautics  
Administration mailing service.
In the interest of safety, compliance  
with the notice, procedures and effective  
date provisions of section 4 of the A d­
ministrative Procedures Act is imprac­
ticable and contrary to the public inter­
est, and therefore, is not required.
Section 507.10 (a) is amended as fol­
lows:
1. 57-13-9 Piper PA-23 as it appeared  
in 23 F. R. 434 is amended by deleting  
all references to P/N 17093-00 (stabi­
lizer—fuselage attachment fitting) that  
appear in the directive; i. e., in Section  
n  a line 10; Section n  c line 8 and Sec­
tion III line 5. Reference AD 58-1-6 for  
material covering P/N 17093-00.
The f ollowing new airworthiness direc­
tives are added:
58-1-1 A ero D esign applies to all A ero  
Commander aircraft with, serial numbers 
231 through 580 except 315, 466, 471, 4 8 5 , 
492, 509, 523, 547, 568, 570, 572, 574, 576’ 
579.'
Compliance required as soon as possible  
but not later than July 1,1958.
A number of failures of the vent lines lo­
cated above the nacelle upper fire shield have  
resulted in the release of fuel and/or fuel  
vapor in the engine compartment creating a  
dangerous fire hazard. These failures are a  
result of interference or chafing between  
wing structure and the carburetor return and  
the fuel tank vent lines; Also, failures have  
occurred at the carburetor vapor return  
elbow located in the upper fire shield.
Replace the portions of the carburetor  
vapor vent and fuel tank vent lines located  
above the upper fire shield with flexible hose  
assemblies, Parts Nos. 6630086-237, 6630086-  
223, and 6630086-229, or equivalent. Securely  
fasten the hose assemblies to the wing struc­
ture with hose clamps to prevent interfer­
ence or chafing.
Replace the existing carburetor vapor re­
turn line elbows located at the upper fire  
shield with anti-rotation fittings, Part N os.  
5630085-21 and 5630085-29, and install upper  
fire shield channels, Part Nos. 5630086-25  
and 5630086-23.
(Additional details relative to this rework  
are included in Aero Design Service Bulletin  
No. 45 dated September 20,1957).
58-1-3 Convair applies to the following  
aircraft equipped with PR-58E5-17 car­
buretors in P&W Double Wasp CB16 and 
17 engines: Convair 440 serial 312  
through 420 and all CV-340 with C V -  
440 nacelles.
Compliance required by first engine over­
haul after March 1, 1958, but not later than  
October 1, 1958.
The PR-58E5— 17 carburetor setting origi­
nally provided in the aircraft has an un­
desirable leaning tendency. To overcome  
this deficiency the PR-58E5-29 carburetor  
setting has been developed and must be in­
corporated in the above aircraft.
Normal fuel metering in carburetors in­
corporating the PR-58E5— 29 “Transport 
Setting” may result in powers lower than  
those employed for aircraft certification. 
This occurs in the high power range with the 
control in the Auto-Rich position in cases 
where the carburetor meters on the rich side 
of the allowable limits. The amount of 
power loss will vary with different carburet­
ors.
Performance information in the C A A  ap­
proved Airplane Flight Manual is based upon  
the maximum certificated power ratings of  
the engine. To obtain full rated power at  
manifold pressure limits for maximum con­
tinuous power, it , is necessary to adjust the  
fuel mixture by the mixture control (takeoff  
power is not adversely affected by use of the  
full rich mixture position). P&W A Engine  
Operation Information Letter No. 28 covers  
this subject in further detail.

The earlier signing-time reading is disclosed and not adopted.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10156 (15 FR 5789 (Federal Register of August 29, 1950)) was signed August 26, 1950. The held text begins with unrelated railroad-list pages of the same Federal Register issue and carries an unrelated sugar regulation after the order; the dossier's clause covered the railroad list's table fragments, so the inventory is corrected to the order's own text. The order designates, under section 179 of the Revised Statutes, the officers who perform the duties of the Secretary of the Interior in case of death, resignation, absence or sickness: the Under Secretary (1(a)), then the ranking Assistant Secretary (1(b)), then the Solicitor (1(c)); paragraph 2 defines the ranking Assistant Secretary; paragraph 3 supersedes Executive Order No. 9866 of June 14, 1947. On 2026-10-14 the designations in paragraphs 1 and 2 are terminated by Executive Order 10753 (23 FR 1107 (Federal Register of February 20, 1958)), signed February 15, 1958 by President Eisenhower, which sets a new order of succession and closes with the sentence “This order supersedes Executive Order” naming Executive Order No. 10156 of August 26, 1950 and its title. That sentence names this order by number and date and has no exception or saving clause. Paragraph 3 was a one-time supersession performed when the order took effect and is terminated on August 26, 1950. The order has no own-terms sunset. The only later instrument in the held corpus that names the order is Executive Order 10753 (the neighbouring Federal Register page of Executive Order 10155 reprints this order's heading, not a later instrument). The Federal Register disposition-note search lists the one hit, Executive Order 10753; the U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit. The superseded Executive Order No. 9866 stays superseded; that is a surviving consequence of paragraph 3 and not a command left to end.

the Airworthiness Directives amended or  
issued during January 1958. Individual  
notice of the Airworthiness Directives  
contained herein has been given to 4  op­
erators and other interested persons who  
are subscribers to a Civil Aeronautics  
Administration mailing service.
In the interest of safety, compliance  
with the notice, procedures and effective  
date provisions of section 4 of the A d­
ministrative Procedures Act is imprac­
ticable and contrary to the public inter­
est, and therefore, is not required.

lows:
1. 57-13-9 Piper PA-23 as it appeared  
in 23 F. R. 434 is amended by deleting  
all references to P/N 17093-00 (stabi­
lizer—fuselage attachment fitting) that  
appear in the directive; i. e., in Section  
n  a line 10; Section n  c line 8 and Sec­
tion III line 5. Reference AD 58-1-6 for  
material covering P/N 17093-00.

tives are added:
58-1-1 A ero D esign applies to all A ero  
Commander aircraft with, serial numbers 
231 through 580 except 315, 466, 471, 4 8 5 , 
492, 509, 523, 547, 568, 570, 572, 574, 576’ 
579.'
Compliance required as soon as possible  
but not later than July 1,1958.
A number of failures of the vent lines lo­
cated above the nacelle upper fire shield have  
resulted in the release of fuel and/or fuel  
vapor in the engine compartment creating a  
dangerous fire hazard. These failures are a  
result of interference or chafing between  
wing structure and the carburetor return and  
the fuel tank vent lines; Also, failures have  
occurred at the carburetor vapor return  
elbow located in the upper fire shield.
Replace the portions of the carburetor  
vapor vent and fuel tank vent lines located  
above the upper fire shield with flexible hose  
assemblies, Parts Nos. 6630086-237, 6630086-  
223, and 6630086-229, or equivalent. Securely  
fasten the hose assemblies to the wing struc­
ture with hose clamps to prevent interfer­
ence or chafing.
Replace the existing carburetor vapor re­
turn line elbows located at the upper fire  
shield with anti-rotation fittings, Part N os.  
5630085-21 and 5630085-29, and install upper  
fire shield channels, Part Nos. 5630086-25  
and 5630086-23.
(Additional details relative to this rework  
are included in Aero Design Service Bulletin  
No. 45 dated September 20,1957).

aircraft equipped with PR-58E5-17 car­
buretors in P&W Double Wasp CB16 and 
17 engines: Convair 440 serial 312  
through 420 and all CV-340 with C V -  
440 nacelles.
Compliance required by first engine over­
haul after March 1, 1958, but not later than  
October 1, 1958.
The PR-58E5— 17 carburetor setting origi­
nally provided in the aircraft has an un­
desirable leaning tendency. To overcome  
this deficiency the PR-58E5-29 carburetor  
setting has been developed and must be in­
corporated in the above aircraft.
Normal fuel metering in carburetors in­
corporating the PR-58E5— 29 “Transport 
Setting” may result in powers lower than  
those employed for aircraft certification. 
This occurs in the high power range with the 
control in the Auto-Rich position in cases 
where the carburetor meters on the rich side 
of the allowable limits. The amount of 
power loss will vary with different carburet­
ors.
Performance information in the C A A  ap­
proved Airplane Flight Manual is based upon  
the maximum certificated power ratings of  
the engine. To obtain full rated power at  
manifold pressure limits for maximum con­
tinuous power, it , is necessary to adjust the  
fuel mixture by the mixture control (takeoff  
power is not adversely affected by use of the  
full rich mixture position). P&W A Engine  
Operation Information Letter No. 28 covers  
this subject in further detail.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The clause continues Executive Order No. 10084, for regulations under sections 206 and 302 of the Act, until October 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950. Executive Order 10174, signed October 23, 1950 and effective November 1, 1950, restated the extension for section 302 alone until January 31, 1951, before the October 31 date arrived. Under the owner ruling on restatements the clause continues, amended, until the parent order ends, so it ends on January 31, 1951 (inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins), with Executive Order 10174 recorded as a later event. Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Each amendment takes effect the day after the earlier date it extends ends, so the dates are read inclusively and leave no gap.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10158 (15 FR 5927 (Federal Register of September 1, 1950)) concerns the order that adopts, as regulations under Titles II, III and V of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, the existing pay regulations, and fixes how long that adoption lasts. Executive Order 10158 was signed August 31, 1950 and becomes effective September 1, 1950. Its only command amends Executive Order No. 10084 (as amended by Executive Orders No. 10098, No. 10118 and No. 10136) so that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 206 and 302 of the Act, it continues in effect until October 31, 1950. Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Each amendment takes effect the day after the earlier date it extends ends, so the dates are read inclusively and leave no gap. The last held instrument is Executive Order 10174 (15 FR 7165 (Federal Register of October 26, 1950)), which continues the order, to the extent it adopts regulations under section 302 of the Act, “until January 31, 1951”. On 2026-10-14 the clause is terminated at that last sunset, January 31, 1951, inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins. The dossier's later-event chain and the held-text search for citations of Executive Order No. 10084 (searched also with a trailing footnote digit) show no later instrument after Executive Order 10174: the Federal Register disposition-note search lists the five amendments named above, and the U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit. A later extension that the held corpus lacks is not excluded, which is the usual limit of a bounded search and is disclosed.

Adopted by the Civil Aeronautics 
Board at its office in Washington, D. C., 
on the 13th day of February 1951.
Under current regulations applicants 
for commercial pilot certificates are re­
quired to meet the second-class physical 
standards. Such standards include a 
requirement for “normal fields of vision” 
which has been interpreted to require 
those applicants to have normal color 
vision. Under current requirements 
student and private pilots who are re­
quired to meet third-class physical 
standards have not had to demonstrate 
normal color vision. An amendment of 
Part 29, being adopted concurrently with 
this amendment, changes the color vi­
sion requirement for the second-class 
physical standard to make it more di­
rectly related to aviation safety, and for
the first time adds a color vision require­
ment to the third-class physical stand­
ards. The amendments provide that 
applicants for all pilot certificates shall 
have the ability to distinguish aviation 
signal red, aviatron signal green, and 
white. (See the amendment of Part 29 
for details with respect to the changed 
requirements and the manner of ad­
ministration thereof.) This amendment 
of Part 20 provides that an applicant 
who is unable to distinguish these avia­
tion signal colors may still be issued a 
pilot certificate, restricted, however, to 
the exercise of the certificate privileges 
under such conditions, or with the use of 
such equipment, as will not require the 
ability to distinguish aviation signal 
colors.
Interested persons have been afforded 
an opportunity to participate in the 
making of this amendment, and due con­
sideration has been given to all relevant 
matter presented.
In consideration of the foregoing the 
Civil Aeronautics Board hereby amends 
Part 20 of the Civil Air Regulations (14 
CFR Part 20 as amended) effective 
March 20, 1951.

ered aircraft.  Applicant shall meet the 
physical standards of the third class

able to distinguish aviation signal red, 
aviation signal green, and white shall be 
issued an airman certificate appropri­
ately endorsed to prohibit the holder 
thereof from exercising the privileges of 
such certificate except under such con­
ditions, or with the use of such equip­
ment, which would not require the 
ability to distinguish such aviation signal 
colors.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The sentence exempts Arthur A. Quinn from compulsory retirement for age “for an indefinite period of time, not extending beyond June 30, 1951”. The order fixes no earlier end event, so the stated date is the latest date the exemption could last and is the best supported end date. It is recorded inclusive (through June 30, 1951); the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins. An earlier lapse, such as separation from office, is not shown by any held source and is disclosed as unestablished.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10215 (16 FR 1703 (Federal Register of February 20, 1951)) was signed February 16, 1951. Its held Federal Register text prints the order number, the title and the signing date. Its only operative command exempts Arthur A. Quinn, Comptroller of Customs with headquarters at New York, New York, from compulsory retirement for age under the Civil Service Retirement Act of May 29, 1930, as amended, under section 204 of the act of June 30, 1932, “for an indefinite period of time, not extending beyond June 30, 1951”. On 2026-10-14 the clause is terminated: by its own words the exemption cannot extend beyond June 30, 1951. The period is described as indefinite but capped, so the cap is the latest date on which the exemption could be in force. No held source shows that the exemption lapsed earlier (for example by Mr. Quinn's separation from office), and none shows any extension: the person-name search of the held order texts found no other order naming him, and the held-text search for the order's number found no citation. The Federal Register disposition-note, U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit naming this order. The best supported date is therefore June 30, 1951, recorded on the inclusive reading, with the possibility of an earlier factual lapse disclosed. The dossier split the sentence into a long fragment and the five-character fragment “1951.”; the inventory is corrected to the single operative sentence.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The sentence exempts Bernice Pyke from compulsory retirement for age, effective as of April 1, 1950, “for an indefinite period of time not extending beyond March 31, 1952, the date on which her present term of office expires”. The cap is the order's own end and equals the date her present term expires, so it is recorded as the end, inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when March 31, 1952 begins. Executive Order 10333 of March 25, 1952 further exempts her for a new indefinite period “not extending beyond the appointment and qualification of her successor”; that is a later extension with its own term and is not treated as an end of this order.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10225 (16 FR 2544 (Federal Register of March 20, 1951)) was signed March 17, 1951. Its held Federal Register text prints the order number, the title and the signing date. Its only operative command exempts Bernice Pyke, Collector of Customs for Customs Collection District No. 41 with headquarters at Cleveland, Ohio, from compulsory retirement for age under the Civil Service Retirement Act of May 29, 1930, as amended, effective as of April 1, 1950 (the order was signed nearly a year after that date), “for an indefinite period of time not extending beyond March 31, 1952, the date on which her present term of office expires”. On 2026-10-14 the clause is terminated by its own terms on March 31, 1952, the date on which her present term of office expires. Executive Order 10333 (17 FR 2705 (Federal Register of March 28, 1952)), signed March 25, 1952, recites this order, says that she was exempted by it for an indefinite period of time not extending beyond March 31, 1952, and further exempts her for an indefinite period “not extending beyond the appointment and qualification of her successor”. That is a later extension by a new order with its own term, recorded as a later event and not as the end of this order; it also shows that the exemption had not lapsed before March 25, 1952. The person-name search found Executive Order 10333 and the neighbouring Federal Register page that also prints this order (Executive Order 10224 on the same page); no other held text names her. The Federal Register disposition-note, U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit naming this order.
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"No earlier end is shown. The exemption's own cap, March 31, 1952, is the end; Executive Order 10333, signed March 25, 1952, treats the exemption as still in place six days before the cap and extends it for a new term. The date recorded is March 31, 1952 on the inclusive reading (the exemption runs through that day); the exclusive reading, under which it ends when that day begins, is the alternative. A later further exemption is a later event with its own date and quotation, not this order's end.","independent_command_check":"The order has a single command with a single cap and no separate continuing duty. Executive Order 10333 creates a new exemption that is not part of this order.","savings_check":"The exemption only allows continued service despite reaching retirement age; the order creates no right that outlives March 31, 1952, has no saving clause, and the bounded searches found no instrument continuing this exemption other than the separate further exemption in Executive Order 10333.","scope_check":"One operative sentence (the exemption, made effective as of April 1, 1950). The recital that the public interest requires it is not a command."}

savings_residuals.reason: The exemption only allows continued service despite reaching retirement age; the order creates no right that outlives March 31, 1952, has no saving clause, and the bounded searches found no instrument continuing this exemption other than the separate further exemption in Executive Order 10333.
